title: Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ to go on display in London
author: Ian Mansfield
content:
Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ to go on display in London
Later this month, Diana, Princess of Wales’s infamous “revenge dress” will go on public display before being offered for sale at auction.
![](https://www.ianvisits.co.uk/articles/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/09/sothebys-to-auction-princess-dianas-revenge-dress-press-release-3.jpg)
The dress owes its fame to the evening of 29th June 1994, when Diana made a showstopping arrival at the Serpentine Gallery for a fundraising dinner hosted by Vanity Fair.
For the evening, she wore a figure-hugging black silk evening dress by Greek designer Christina Stambolian.
That same evening, Prince Charles, from whom Diana had been separated for almost two years, was due to admit on national television that he had been unfaithful. The revelations had been leaked several days earlier, so Diana knew that whatever she did while the programme was being watched by millions would inevitably be interpreted as a response.
She could easily have cancelled her appearance at the Serpentine dinner. Instead, she attended — and made a last-minute change to her wardrobe.
A more traditional Valentino gown was set aside in favour of Stambolian’s black dress, which Diana had bought three years earlier but had considered too daring to wear in public. On that historic evening, she evidently decided its moment had arrived.
The dress quickly became one of the few garments to transcend fashion and enter the collective cultural imagination. Dubbed Diana’s “revenge dress” almost overnight, it was seen as a powerful expression of confidence at a moment when the princess was under intense public scrutiny.
The dress was sold in 1997 and is now back up for sale – if you have the very deep pockets to afford it.
However, for the rest of us, it will go on display at Sotheby’s auction house in a free exhibition.
The exhibition runs from Friday 18th to Thursday 24th September at Sotheby’s on Bond Street.
Sotheby’s is open Mon to Fri from 10am to 5pm. Sotheby’s is usually closed at weekends, but a spokesperson said that whether they will open at the weekend for this exhibition is to be confirmed.
The auction takes place in December.
summary: Princess Diana's famous "revenge dress" is set to go on public display at Sotheby's in London before being put up for auction in December. Diana originally wore the figure-hugging black silk dress by designer Christina Stambolian on June 29, 1994, the same evening Prince Charles admitted to infidelity on television. The garment will be exhibited for free from Friday 18th to Thursday 24th September at Sotheby’s on Bond Street.
key_points: Princess Diana wore the black silk dress on June 29, 1994, at a Serpentine Gallery dinner.
The dress was worn the same night Prince Charles publicly admitted to infidelity on television.
Diana had purchased the dress three years earlier from Greek designer Christina Stambolian.
The dress will be exhibited for free at Sotheby’s on Bond Street from September 18 to September 24.
The dress is scheduled to be sold at an auction in December.

title: The 10 London art exhibitions we’re most excited about in autumn 2026
author: Rosie Hewitson
content:
[title]
London summer may be drawing to a close, but if you’re already dreading the day when you have to retrieve your chunky knits from that old suitcase under your bed, then allow us to give you something – or, in fact, 10 things – to look forward to as the nights get darker.
London’s parks are looking a little lifeless after a season of back-to-back heatwaves and non-stop festivals, but the capital’s art scene is bursting into life. Autumn is unquestionably the best season of the year for art-lovers, with loads of art fairs in town – including major industry fixtures Frieze and Frieze Masters – and blockbuster exhibitions opening at the city’s biggest galleries.
From renaissance portraiture to contemporary fashion photography, major impressionists to minimalist pioneers, there are so many great shows on the horizon that it’ll require some deft planning to pack them all in. So grab your diary and read on for our pick of the best exhibitions coming to London this autumn.
10 London art exhibitions we’re most excited about in autumn 2026
![Still from ‘Enclosure’ by Jenkin Van Zyl](https://media.timeout.com/images/106446187/image.webp) 
Named one of Time Out's young London artists to watch a few years back, Jenkin Van Zyl asks pertinent questions about the systems we create for ourselves and the human need for self-preservation. His immersive installations cast visitors in a variety of unsettling scenarios: his upcoming show at Somerset House Studios is a large-scale work where visitors move through ‘facility’, past fairground signage, holograms, inflatable cocoons and decaying ephemera.
Somerset House. Sept 24-Nov 29. Free.
Tate’s 2026 programming has been big on the 90s! Following on Tate Modern’s fabulous retrospective on YBA Tracey Emin, Tate Britain’s blockbuster autumn show examines the British art, fashion, photography and pop culture in the final decade of the last millennium. Curated by former British Vogue editor Edward Enninful, it will feature photography from the likes of Juergen Teller, Nick Knight and Corinne Day, iconic Westwood and McQueen looks, and era-defining art by Damien Hirst, Gillian Wearing, and Yinka Shonibare.
Tate Britain. Oct 8-Feb 14 2027. £22.
![Salman Toor, The Bar on East 13th, 2019, Oil on panel © Salman Toor](https://media.timeout.com/images/106314825/image.webp) 
The Courtauld hosts a first solo European exhibition for Pakistan-born, New York-based artist Salman Toor from October. Toor explores the struggle and desire for belonging, both culturally and emotionally through this collection of 19 paintings, which are inspired by both his personal experiences as a South Asian queer man and his admiration for baroque and 18th-century masters.
Courtauld Gallery. Oct 2-Jan 10 2027. £18.
His reputation might not be up there with Monet and Degas, but London’s art lovers go mad for a bit of French impressionism. It’s a little surprising that the capital hasn’t hosted an exhibition on one of its leading figures, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, since the National Gallery’s 2007 show on his landscapes nearly 20 years ago. The gallery’s new exhibition is doubly timely, what with the high-profile heist that recently took place at the Musée Renoir in the south of France, and will feature several of Renoir’s most iconic works, including the 1876 painting ‘Bal au Moulin de la Galette’, exhibited for the first time ever in the UK. Here’s hoping security is a little less lax at the Trafalgar Square institution.
National Gallery. Oct 3-Jan 31 2027. From £20.
![Pierre-Auguste Renoir, ‘Dance at the Moulin de la Galette’ (1876)](https://media.timeout.com/images/106317828/image.webp) 
The late American painter Robert Ryman was a master of minimalism, even if he was reluctant to apply the term to his own work. His signature white-on-white paintings urge the viewer to look closely at his brushstrokes, in all their tactile glory, and to enjoy the subtlety and nuance of the varied effects he achieved. He’s not often shown in the UK, with this Barbican exhibition constituting a first major airing here in over 30 years. There’ll be 60 paintings on display, spanning his six-decade career.
Barbican Gallery Oct 8-Feb 28 2027. Price TBC.
Best known for his eye-popping, fantastical fashion photography for titles including British Vogue and i-D, British photographer Tim Walker has spent the past five years photographing the nation’s LGBTQ+ trailblazers in preparation for this major exhibition at the National Portrait Gallery, his first show in London since the V&A’s acclaimed exhibition in 2019.
The National Portrait Gallery. Oct 9-Feb 7 2027. Price TBC.
![Katsushika Hokusai, ‘Sekiya Village on the Sumida River’, (1830-1833). The Iuchi Collection, on deposit at The National Museum of Western Art, Tokyo.](https://media.timeout.com/images/106445886/image.webp) 
Even if you know absolutely nothing about Japanese printmaker Katsushika Hokusai, there’s a good chance you know ‘The Great Wave’. Depicting Mount Fuji dwarfed by a huge wave, it’s the most iconic work of his 1831 series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, which is widely regarded as one of the greatest achievements in the history of printmaking thanks to its embrace of vivid pigments and ukiyo-e woodblock techniques. It’s rarely seen outside of Japan in its entirety, and this exhibition marks the first time in the UK that the complete set of 46 prints (the original 36, plus the 10 expanded works) have been brought together.
Dulwich Picture Gallery. Oct 20-Jan 17 2027. From £21.50.
London’s photography fans might have been dismayed that the major Nan Goldin retrospective that has been touring around Europe over the last few years never made it across the channel, but this brand new show at the Hayward Gallery should soften the blow. The American photographer and activist’s first institutional exhibition in the UK since 2022, its main focus is You Never Did Anything Wrong Part I (2024) and Part II (2026), a pair of abstract films scored by the composer Mica Levi and screened in bespoke spaces designed with architect Hala Wardé.
Hayward Gallery. Nov 24-Mar 14 2027. From £19.
![Jan van Eyck, ‘The Arnolfini Portrait’ (1434). Oil on wood.](https://media.timeout.com/images/106445885/image.webp) 
Before Jan Van Eyck came along in the 1430s, depictions of people were mostly (but not always) rigid, flat and unrealistic, representing general religious archetypes rather than real-life figures. The early renaissance painter basically invented portraiture as we know it today, capturing all the intimate details of craftsmen, merchants and members of his family, from subtle stubble to flushed cheeks to bloodshot eyes. This landmark exhibition will mark the first time that all nine of the artist’s surviving portraits are on display together – the pieces are so fragile that they very rarely travel – so consider this a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.
National Gallery. Nov 21-Apr 11 2027. Price TBC.
Take a break from rainy autumnal London and pretend you’re taking in the sea air on the Côte d’Azur at this Royal Academy exhibition. Spanning impressionists, post-umpressionists and modernists, it brings together artworks a whole bunch of greats, including Monet, Braque, Picasso, Matisse, Cézanne, Renoir and Klein, to explore how the glorious natural light and sparkling azure sea of the riviera was inextricably linked to the rise of modern art.
Royal Academy. Oct 2-Jan 31 2027. From £24.
Plus, the Courtauld Gallery just announced its 2027 exhibition programme – featuring Paula Rego, JMW Turner, Georgia O’Keeffe and Rubens
Get the latest and greatest from the Big Smoke – from news and reviews to events and trends. Just follow our Time Out London WhatsApp channel.
Stay in the loop: sign up for our free Time Out London newsletter for the best of the city, straight to your inbox
summary: London's autumn 2026 art season features a diverse lineup of major exhibitions across the city's leading galleries. Highlights include immersive installations, rare historical collections, and showcases dedicated to fashion, photography, impressionism, and early renaissance portraiture.
key_points: Somerset House Studios will host an immersive, large-scale installation by Jenkin Van Zyl.
Tate Britain is presenting an exhibition on 1990s British art, fashion, and pop culture curated by Edward Enninful.
The National Gallery will display Renoir's 'Bal au Moulin de la Galette' for the first time in the UK.
Dulwich Picture Gallery is bringing together Katsushika Hokusai's complete set of 46 prints from the 'Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji' series.
The National Gallery will feature all nine surviving portraits by early renaissance painter Jan Van Eyck.

title: Man fights for life after 'machete attack' in Bromley leaves four in hospital - live
author: Matt Watts; Nicholas Cecil; Megan Howe; Niva Yadav
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![Helicopter seen hovering above Bromley after four stabbed on high street](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/10/19/52dc03ec7ab1c3cf8c2d872d1ab6b72bY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5MTQ5NzU1-2.85808809.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75) A man is in critical condition and three others in hospital after being stabbed in a knife attack in a KFC restaurant in south London. The stabbings in Bromley High Street followed reports of a number of people being seen in the area carrying machetes. Police confirmed they responded to reports of an “altercation” at around 2.15pm on Thursday. They found the four men who had been stabbed and London Ambulance Service said they were all taken to hospital. One is in a critical condition. Seven people have been arrested and remain in police custody. Forensic officers and a crime scene photographer were later seen working inside and outside the KFC restaurant on the High Street and there were evidence markers on the floor. The fast food chain confirmed a “serious incident” took place inside their restaurant. Scroll down for the latest updates. Live updates 'Boys running with long knives' says cafe worker A cafe worker reported seeing “boys running with long knives” at the scene of the crime on Thursday evening. Speaking to the Metro, the unnamed worked said: “People were scattering everywhere. I was thinking it could be a terrorist attack. “Everyone was terrified.” The cafe worker is just one eyewitness who reported seeing long blades on Bromley High Street yesterday. A worker at KFC told the same outlet that all staff were “unharmed” in the incident. ![Police at the scene in Bromley after four people have been taken to hospital after reports of a stabbing in south-east London, emergency services said (James Manning/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/10/19/52dc03ec7ab1c3cf8c2d872d1ab6b72bY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5MTQ5NzU1-2.85808809.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640) Lib Dem councillor praises "robust" police response Liberal Democrat councillor Graeme Casey has praised the police for their swift response to the incident. He said: "We're very grateful because, of course, one of the big problems we have in London is our police are quite thinly stretched, so to have had such a robust response in such a short space of time is really to the credit of all the blue-light services involved." In a separate social media post, Cllr Casey said a Section 35 dispersal order was in place until 2am on Friday. Police say no wider threat to the public The Metropolitan Police confirmed yesterday that there was no wider threat to the public. Forensic investigators were seen at the scene on Bromley High Street yesterday, while a police cordon remained in place for the afternoon. ![Forensic investigators at the scene after four people were stabbed (James Manning/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/10/19/c85053ce443eb5914f7e19ec501ef33eY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5MTQ5ODQ2-2.85808855.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640) Man fighting for his life Four men were stabbed in the incident on Bromley High Street yesterday afternoon. Seven men have since been arrested in connection. One of the victims is understood to be in a critical condition, while the three others remain in hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. ![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/11/11/01M2640HF4XCD3AKJ7A79MY6M4.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640) Images show large response from emergency services Images on social media shared yesterday show a large emergency response at the scene in Bromley. The London Ambulance Service, Metropolitan Police, and Air Ambulance service were all dispatched to Bromley High Street following reports of a stabbing. Mayor of London aware of quadruple stabbing The Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan is understood to be aware of the quadruple stabbing that took place in Bromley yesterday afternoon. A spokesperson for the Mayor’s Office said: “The Mayor is aware of the incident in Bromley in which four men have been stabbed, one of whom has been left in a critical condition. “Thanks to swift work from Met police officers, seven men have already been arrested. There is not believed to be any wider threat to the public but police enquiries continue. “There is no place for this violence in London and the Mayor is calling on anyone with information linked to this incident to contact the police on 101 or call Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111. There is no honour in staying silent.” ![

Sir Sadiq Khan is expected to decide next year whether to stand for re-election as London Mayor in 2028

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/03/14/01M1KBH1NTHYDTC0Q4A7P15533.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640) 'Loud bang and people running from KFC', says local barber Multiple eyewitness reports have emerged since the stabbings on Bromley High Street yesterday. Some reports have claimed long blades resembling “machetes” were involved in the altercation. George Ioannu, a barber working at Antonio’s Male Grooming next to the KFC, told the Guardian: “I heard a really loud bang and people running from KFC.” He added that an elderly woman ran into the shop crying. He then locked the door to shelter the lady. ![

Forensic investigators on the scene in Bromley

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/10/18/01M263KKAS26BPQCGS6Z7H84XJ.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640) Where did the stabbing take place? The incident is understood to have taken place at a KFC on Bromley High Street. The fast food restaurant is located just a short walk away from Bromley South railway station, on the Southern Railways line. Opposite the restaurant is a large TK Maxx, while it is also adjacent to an alleyway. The Guardian reported that people ran down the alleyway as they fled from the KFC at the time of the incident. Around 15 bus routes serve the high street - all of which were diverted following the incident. What did the London Ambulance Service say? The London Ambulance Service - which has just reported its busiest summer on record - was called to the scene on Thursday evening. A statement read: “We were called at 2.19pm [on September 10] to reports of a stabbing on Bromley High Street, BR1. “We sent ambulance crews, a paramedic in a fast response car, an incident response officers, and an advanced paramedic. We also dispatched London’s Air Ambulance. “We treated four patients at the scene and took them all to hospital.” ![The scene in Bromley after four people were taken to hospital following reports of a stabbing (James Manning/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/10/18/62ba2af15e6ac965e7dbec7ed80bf56cY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5MTQ1OTI5-2.85808710.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640) Everything we know so far about the Bromley stabbings It has been almost 20 hours since four men were stabbed on Bromley High Street in south-east London yesterday afternoon. One of those men is in critical condition in hospital, while the three others are being treated for non-life-threatening injuries. Seven men have since been arrested in connection with the incident. Paramedics, the Metropolitan Police, and the London Air Ambulance was called to the usually bustling high street yesterday at around 2.20pm following reports of a stabbing. Eyewitnesses reported seeing a machete at the scene. The incident is understood to have taken place at a KFC restaurant, with the fast food chain confirming “a serious incident” had taken place. A police cordon was in place, rendering the high street shut, but has since been lifted. ![The scene in Bromley after four people were taken to hospital following reports of a stabbing (James Manning/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/10/18/62ba2af15e6ac965e7dbec7ed80bf56cY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5MTQ1OTI5-2.85808710.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640)
summary: Four men were hospitalized following a knife attack inside a KFC restaurant on Bromley High Street in south London, with one victim currently in critical condition. Police responded to reports of an altercation involving individuals carrying machetes around 2:15 pm on Thursday. Seven men have been arrested in connection with the incident, and authorities confirmed there is no wider threat to the public.
key_points: Four men were stabbed during an incident inside a KFC restaurant on Bromley High Street.
One victim is in critical condition, while three others are being treated for non-life-threatening injuries.
Seven men have been arrested and remain in police custody.
Eyewitnesses reported seeing individuals carrying long knives or machetes.
Police and emergency services, including the London Air Ambulance, responded to the scene, and authorities confirmed there is no wider threat to the public.

title: Mapped: 20mph limits sweep inner London as outer boroughs hold out
author: Megan Howe
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![The London Question: Should there be more 20mph roads in London?](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/10/18/04/Screenshot-2026-09-10-at-16-00-17.png?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
![TfL data shows the speed limits in each London borough](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/10/18/04/Screenshot-2026-09-10-at-16-00-17.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
If you head towards outer London, the picture changes dramatically, with swathes of road remaining at 30mph and higher.
Bromley, Bexley and Havering stand out as areas where a number of roads remain at 30mph, while boroughs including Croydon, Brent and Harrow show a more mixed picture as 20mph zones continue to creep in.
Further towards the capital’s fringes, faster 40mph, 50mph and even 60mph routes are more prominent.
Seventy-two per cent of Greenwich roads already have 20mph zones, but the Council is looking to expand this in the interest of safety and to simplify its roads for drivers.
According to Transport for London data, more than three quarters of serious injuries or deaths on Greenwich roads in the last 10 years were on roads of more than 20mph.
There will be some exceptions to the rule, and no final decisions have been made yet.
But Greenwich’s cabinet member Calum O’Byrne Mulligan said the move would “save lives and create safer, more welcoming streets” while “making it easier for drivers to understand and follow” road rules.
According to the London Boroughs Healthy Streets Scorecard, which ranks all 32 of London’s boroughs based on how well they encourage safe and sustainable travel, 61.7% of borough-managed roads across London are now 20mph, up from 60.9% in 2025.
![20mph limit](https://static.standard.co.uk/2022/02/24/14/TRANSPORT%2020%20201442.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Nineteen boroughs have reached 95% or more, while Bromley, Hillingdon, Bexley and Havering remain below 10%.
The topic of 20mph zones has long been a contentious one. Supporters argue the expansion of 20mph limits is necessary to save lives on Britain’s roads, while critics say they make driving more frustrating, causing awkward acceleration and leaving drivers feeling the need to constantly check their speedometers for fear of fines.
Read More
Among vulnerable groups, the findings were even more striking, with child fatalities falling by 75 per cent in the areas studied.
Jeremy Leach from campaign group 20's Plenty for Us said: "Greenwich has done a great job in recent years in making its residential roads safer with 20mph limits.
“But, as with most of London, it is those busy main roads where people and vehicles mix in large numbers such as high streets, town centres and public transport hubs where the vast majority of road casualties happen.
“20mph limits are proven to reduce casualties and the good news for people in Greenwich is that main roads with 20mph limits will be safer, quieter, calmer and easier to cross and more people will feel safe to use shops and services in their local area."
But opponents argue that lower speed limits, combined with Low Traffic Neighbourhoods (LTNs) and clean-air schemes, are making driving through the capital increasingly slow and frustrating.
Tradespeople and taxi drivers are among those who say the restrictions come with a financial cost. They argue that longer journeys mean fewer service calls, deliveries and fares can be completed over the course of a working day.
Dave Barnes, a Taxpayers’ Alliance representative from Islington previously described the scheme as a “complete waste of money”, adding “it will make life more difficult and slow everything down.”
For businesses covering long distances across London, they say those lost hours translate into higher operating costs which will ultimately be passed on to customers.
The Conservative party has pledged to scrap blanket 20mph zones, claiming there is a “war on drivers” and that these zones have slowed “whole towns to a crawl while doing little for real safety”.
Shadow Transport Secretary Richard Holden previously said: “Town halls have spent years waging a war on the very people who get up early, drive to work and keep the economy turning.”
There is clearly a stark divide, not only on London's inner and outer borough map, but over what the capital's streets should prioritise — keeping traffic moving or slowing it down in the name of safety.
summary: Inner London is largely sweeping toward 20mph speed limits while outer boroughs retain faster roads, reflecting a divide between safety advocates and critics. Supporters argue that lower limits save lives and reduce casualties, particularly among vulnerable groups, whereas opponents claim the restrictions frustrate drivers, increase business costs, and slow travel. Data shows that 61.7% of borough-managed roads across London are now 20mph.
key_points: Inner London boroughs are widely adopting 20mph limits, while outer boroughs like Bromley, Bexley, and Havering maintain higher speed limits.
Transport for London data indicates that over 75% of serious injuries or deaths on Greenwich roads in the last decade occurred on roads exceeding 20mph.
Supporters argue that 20mph limits save lives and create safer streets, while critics claim they increase travel times, cause frustration, and raise operating costs for businesses.
According to the London Boroughs Healthy Streets Scorecard, 61.7% of borough-managed roads across London are now 20mph.

title: London tourism tax capped at 5%, BBC understands
author: James W Kelly
content:
![Pedestrians walk past the illuminated entrance sign for The Ritz London on a sunny day.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/929/cpsprodpb/b321/live/52e71bd0-ad07-11f1-beae-535b95a24b3e.jpg)
Plans for a tourist levy in London may be capped although no confirmation has been made yet
- Published
London's tourism levy will be capped at 5% of the cost of accommodation, the BBC understands.
Sir Sadiq Khan said he "strongly" welcomed plans set to be formally unveiled by the government later granting mayors in England the power to set an uncapped overnight visitors' levy - often referred to as a tourism tax.
A source at City Hall told BBC London that officials had not landed on an exact figure for the capital but that it would be no higher than 5%.
An industry body said the levy could put tourists off visiting London, while Conservative-led Westminster Council called for boroughs to keep half the funds raised in their area.
The government will provide more details on the policy, first announced last November, after the Housing Secretary Angela Rayner meets mayors virtually at No 10 North on Thursday afternoon.
Under the proposals, local leaders would decide how the revenue raised should be reinvested.
![Keir Starmer and London Mayor Sadiq Khan standing side-by-side during a press event in a control room.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/849/cpsprodpb/850b/live/99cac630-ad09-11f1-a6a8-e924739dac6d.jpg)
The tourist tax policy was first announced by former PM Keir Starmer last year
The mayor of London said: "I strongly welcome the government giving London the power to introduce an Overnight Visitor Levy. This needs to happen sooner rather than later.
"London's visitor economy is a huge success story, supporting jobs, businesses and investment across the capital and the wider country, and I have long argued that London should have the same flexibility as other major global cities to raise and invest funding locally."
Sir Sadiq added that a "well-designed, modest levy" could fund the growth of "London's offer to visitors".
The levy could be in place by March 2028, according to a government document published in July, when Prime Minister Andy Burnham reiterated his commitment to the policy as part of his wider devolution agenda.
Charges of a similar nature already exist across Europe, with the revenue used to fund local services.
Groups representing the tourism trade have warned about the impact of the tax and called for consistency in how it operates across different regions.
![Close-up portrait of Allen Simpson wearing glasses and a dark blue top during an interview.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1536/cpsprodpb/70ac/live/fecbdc40-ad09-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
Allen Simpson says hospitality jobs are "at risk" with the levy
Allen Simpson, chief executive of the trade body, said a tourism tax introduced in Edinburgh in July was "already having damaging effects" and said jobs could be at risk in communities that rely on tourism and hospitality.
"I would say to those people in these communities that their jobs are now at risk," Simpson told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
Analysis released in January by Central London Forward found a hypothetical 3% tourist levy in London could raise more than Â£350m.
Paul Swaddle, Westminster Council's leader, said VAT rates for hotels in other European cities were "significantly lower and the total tax burden is lower", so the tourist levy could make Westminster hotels less competitive.
In France, which has the same 20% standard VAT rate as the UK, hotel stays are taxed at a 10% reduced rate with many cities applying their own local tourist levy.
Several other European countries apply a similar reduced VAT rate to hotel stays.
"If the levy is to be raised, local authorities need to keep at least half to be spent locally for services that benefit visitors, such as keeping the streets clean and safe," Swaddle said.
He said the cost of supporting the "visitor and commuter economy in Westminster" is estimated at Â£115m.
London Councils, which represents the capital's 33 local authorities, has also called for "boroughs to retain a fair share of revenues".
City Hall and the government have not laid out how the levy would be collected, distributed or spent.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: London's upcoming tourism levy is understood to be capped at 5% of accommodation costs, according to BBC sources. The government is granting English mayors the power to set an overnight visitors' levy to reinvest locally, a plan strongly welcomed by London Mayor Sadiq Khan. However, industry bodies and local councils have expressed concerns that the tax could make hotels less competitive, put hospitality jobs at risk, and impact tourism.
key_points: London's tourism tax is understood to be capped at no higher than 5% of accommodation costs.
Mayor Sadiq Khan strongly welcomed the government's plan to grant mayors the power to introduce the levy.
Industry bodies and trade representatives warned the tax could put tourism and hospitality jobs at risk.
Westminster Council and London Councils called for local authorities to retain a fair share of the revenue raised.

title: Bromley stabbing: One man in critical condition as seven arrested
author: Amy Clarke
content:
![Police stand nearby to the KFC](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/cdcd/live/99c80970-ad3d-11f1-85f8-e90160a10ad0.jpg)
KFC confirmed that a "serious incident" took place at the restaurant
- Published
Seven people have been arrested after four men were stabbed in south-east London, the Metropolitan Police has said.
One of the men remains in a critical condition in hospital, while the other three are being treated for injuries that are not believed to be life-threatening.
Paramedics and the London Air Ambulance were called at about 14:20 BST to Bromley High Street, where one eyewitness reported seeing a man wielding a machete.
A KFC spokesperson confirmed a "serious incident" had taken place at its Bromley High Street restaurant and an altercation had begun there. The company said it was assisting police and "supporting our team members and customers at this difficult time".
![Shot from a helicopter of scene on Bromley High Street with London Fire Brigade at the scene and police cordon in place](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/3687/live/0cda6c80-ad31-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.png)
Paramedics were sent to Bromley High Street on Thursday afternoon
An eyewitness, who did not want to be named, said: "I saw a fight breaking out at the door of KFC; people involved were partly inside and outside.
"A male in a grey tracksuit pulled out a machete and ran further into KFC holding it up in the air, at which point most people around KFC started running away, including my friend and I.
"I didn't turn around until we got to the shopping centre where I saw him running away with someone down a road."
![Shot of the high street through a window with London Fire Brigade in attendance and a police cordon in place.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1376/cpsprodpb/bade/live/bb6c19f0-ad32-11f1-9bc8-3509bd1a4ead.jpg)
Police said there was no wider threat to the public
Georgiana, the manager of Merkur Slots gambling shop, said she saw "a fight spill out" on to the High Street.
She said she became "very worried", and locked three customers inside the premises to wait for the situation to calm down.
She said the customers remained inside and that the shop was still closed.
Watch: BBC reports from scene of south-east London stabbing
Vinnie Guadagnino, who lives on Bromley High Street, said he saw a large emergency response with multiple police cars and about 10 officers on foot.
"Police cars kept coming, then within the next half hour there were multiple fire engines and people gathering.
"Then there was a drone overhead and helicopters and an air ambulance - so a massive emergency service response."
![Satellite map of central Bromley, south-east London, showing the marked location of an incident in the town centre. Nearby landmarks labelled include The Glades shopping centre to the north-east and Bromley South railway station to the south. An inset map of London highlights Bromley's location within the capital.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/6236/live/3e9d6e20-ad36-11f1-b1d1-571ed4d7ff2c.jpg)
![Police cordons block part of Bromley High Street as officers stand outside businesses near a KFC. A marked police car and police van are parked within the cordoned area, with the street largely empty behind the tape.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/be83/live/fc0fa5d0-ad32-11f1-bc1f-3f186ca4140c.png)
A cordon remains in place at the scene
Bromley High Street is currently closed both ways from Ringers Road to Ethelbert Road.
Police remain at the scene and say there is not believed to be any wider threat to the public.
![Forensics investigations in blue suits walk through the crime, with the yellow cordon behind them.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/9530/live/09c70dd0-ad38-11f1-9bc8-3509bd1a4ead.jpg)
Forensic investigators at the scene on Bromley High Street
Peter Fortune, Conservative MP for Bromley and Biggin Hill, said on X that residents "would have safety concerns" and he would remain in contact with the police as they investigate.
Liberal Democrat councillor Graeme Casey said: "We're very grateful because, of course, one of the big problems we have in London is our police are quite thinly stretched, so to have had such a robust response in such a short space of time is really to the credit of all the blue-light services involved."
![Two youths stand on Bromley High Street near a bus stop and shopfronts as they speak to reporters. Store signage, including FrasersPlus and Blacks, is visible in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1800/cpsprodpb/380c/live/c6b0b7c0-ad38-11f1-9bc8-3509bd1a4ead.jpg)
Witnesses Matias Alil and Fergal Hickey saw the commotion
Matias Alil described the reaction on the street. He said: "It was terrible. We saw a massive commotion and something going on in KFC. It was really scary, to be honest."
Fergal Hickey added: "You can see the police out there have the situation under control, so you don't really need to be too anxious about it but it's still pretty crazy to see it when it happens."
summary: Seven people have been arrested after four men were stabbed following an altercation that began at a KFC on Bromley High Street in south-east London. Paramedics, the London Air Ambulance, and a large emergency service response attended the scene, where one man was left in a critical condition and three others sustained injuries not believed to be life-threatening. Police stated there is no wider threat to the public, and a cordon remains in place while investigations continue.
key_points: Seven people were arrested following a stabbing incident on Bromley High Street.
Four men were injured, with one remaining in a critical condition in hospital.
An eyewitness reported seeing a man wielding a machete during an altercation that started at a KFC restaurant.
Emergency services, including police, paramedics, and an air ambulance, responded to the scene in large numbers.
Police confirmed there is no wider threat to the public.

title: Bromley stabbing: Man critical as four hurt on high street 'machete attack' - updates
author: Matt Watts; Nicholas Cecil; Megan Howe
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![Helicopter seen hovering above Bromley after four stabbed on high street](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/10/18/01M263KKAS26BPQCGS6Z7H84XJ.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75) A man is in critical condition and three others in hospital after being stabbed in a knife attack on a high street in south London. The stabbings in Bromley followed reports of a number of people being seen in the area carrying machetes. Police confirmed they responded to reports of an “altercation” in Bromley High Street at around 2.15pm. They found the four men who had been stabbed and London Ambulance Service said they were all taken to hospital. One is in a critical condition. Seven people have been arrested and remain in police custody. Scroll down for the latest updates. Live updates In Photos: Pictures show forensics and officers at the scene Forensics and police officers have been pictured at the scene of a stabbing in Bromley. Four men have been taken to hospital with injuries, including one who is in critical condition. A police cordon has been put in place and officers remain at the scene offering support to members of the local community. ![The scene in Bromley after four people were taken to hospital (James Manning/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/10/18/a6fc72bca4336e61a98b4b895c860c11Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5MTQ2MDY1-2.85808711.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640) ![The scene in Bromley after four people were taken to hospital following reports of a stabbing (James Manning/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/10/18/62ba2af15e6ac965e7dbec7ed80bf56cY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5MTQ1OTI5-2.85808710.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640) ![

The scene after four people were stabbed on Bromley High Street

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/10/17/13/Screenshot-2026-09-10-180638.jpeg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640) ![

Forensic investigators on the scene in Bromley

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/10/18/01M263KKAS26BPQCGS6Z7H84XJ.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640) Fight reportedly broke out at KFC Eyewitnesses, speaking to the Daily Mail, claim a fight broke out at KFC on Bromley High Street before spilling out into the street. A witness described seeing “a lot of blood”. A bus driver who arrived at the scene moments after the attack said the victims had been attacked with a “zombie knife”. ![Police at the scene of the incident in Bromley (James Manning/PA)](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/10/18/84b8808fbd6a8f1aff075e56d46f255aY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5MTQ2MDEw-2.85808809.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640) Resident on the high street recalls huge police response Vinnie Guadagnino, who lives on the high street, said he saw a huge police response to the incident with several cars and at least ten officers on foot. He told the BBC: “Police cars kept coming, then within the next half hour there were multiple fire engines and people gathering. “Then there was a drone overhead and helicopters and an air ambulance - so a massive emergency service response.” What has the London Ambulance Service said? Paramedics from the London Ambulance Service were called to reports of a stabbing on Bromley High Street at 2.19pm this afternoon. Ambulance crews, a paramedic in a fast response car, an incident response officer, an advanced paramedic and London’s Air Ambulance were dispatched to the scene, the service said. Four patients were treated at the scene and three of them were taken to hospital. First picture from the scene A picture of the aftermath of the stabbing has been shared online. It shows police and members of the London Fire Brigade in attendance and a section of the high street cordoned off. Bystanders stand at the police cordon as officers begin their investigation into the incident. Mayor says 'no place for this violence in London' The Mayor of London Lord Sadiq Khan has said “there is no place for this violence in London. A spokesperson for the mayor said: “The Mayor is aware of the incident in Bromley in which four men have been stabbed, one of whom has been left in a critical condition. “Thanks to swift work from Met police officers, seven men have already been arrested. There is not believed to be any wider threat to the public but police enquiries continue. “There is no place for this violence in London and the Mayor is calling on anyone with information linked to this incident to contact the police on 101 or call Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111. There is no honour in staying silent.” ![

Mayor of London Sadiq Khan

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/06/20/01M1P2XAZAEHJDDTMBA12DVDK5.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=640) 'Men with machetes running around stabbing people' Messages were put out on social media urging people not to go to Bromley because of the 'machete' knife attacks. One user said he had been phoned by a friend alerting him to the stabbings. Reform London Mayoral candidate reacts Laila Cunningham has reacted to the “horrific attack” saying it has made her “angry”. Writing on X she said: “what makes me so angry is that those in charge keep telling Londoners that everything is fine. That London is safe. That somehow what we are seeing with our own eyes isn’t really happening. It is happening.” 'No wider threat to the public' Police have said they do not believe there is a wider threat to the public following the incident. Seven people remain in custody after being arrested following the stabbings. Peter Fortune MP, Member of Parliament for Bromley and Biggin Hill, said : “I know that many local residents will have safety concerns.” Footage shows air ambulance over Bromley after stabbings London Ambulance Service confirmed the Air Ambulance was sent to the scene. Footage shared online has shown it in the skies above Bromley.
summary: Four men were hospitalized following a stabbing attack on Bromley High Street in south London, with one victim currently in critical condition. Police responded to reports of an altercation involving individuals seen carrying machetes and have since arrested seven men who remain in custody. Emergency services, including the air ambulance, attended the scene, and officials stated there is no belief of a wider threat to the public.
key_points: Four men were stabbed in an attack on Bromley High Street following reports of people carrying machetes.
One victim is in a critical condition and three others were taken to hospital.
Seven men have been arrested and remain in police custody in connection with the incident.
Emergency responders including the London Ambulance Service and London's Air Ambulance attended the scene.
Police and the Mayor of London confirmed there is no believed wider threat to the public.

title: Two arrested in London on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service
author: Henry Moore
content:
![A triangular New Scotland Yard sign outside the Metropolitan Police offices in London.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/d4c6/live/1fa03200-2adc-11f1-934f-036468834728.jpg)
- Published
Two people have been arrested in London on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service, the Metropolitan Police has said.
A 60-year-old man and 42-year-old woman were arrested at properties in London on Wednesday as part of an investigation into suspected National Security Act (NSA) offences.
The suspects, who were both held on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service, have been released on bail under strict conditions until late October, the Met said.
Police said the arrests were not "connected to any of the incidents or attacks" linked to Jewish and Iranian communities across London earlier this year.
The arrests took place following two searches carried out at properties in north and north-west London in June, the Met added.
Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said she knows "news of these arrests will come as a concern to some members of the public" but stressed she does "not believe there to be any imminent threat to the wider public".
She added: "We've seen a marked increase in the tempo of our work linked to national security and state threats over the past year and this investigation is a continuation of that.
"As we've shown here, if we suspect any activity could threaten the safety of the UK or the public, then we will not hesitate to take action."
She added the UK's terror threat level was severe and called for people to be vigilant.
summary: Two individuals were arrested in London on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service under the National Security Act. The 60-year-old man and 42-year-old woman were released on bail until late October under strict conditions. Police stated that the arrests are not connected to earlier attacks on Jewish and Iranian communities in London and that there is no imminent threat to the wider public.
key_points: A 60-year-old man and a 42-year-old woman were arrested in London on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service.
The arrests were made as part of an investigation into suspected National Security Act offences.
Both suspects have been released on bail under strict conditions until late October.
Police confirmed the arrests are unrelated to recent incidents involving Jewish and Iranian communities in London.
Counter Terrorism Policing stated there is no imminent threat to the wider public, though the UK's terror threat level remains severe.

title: Sadiq Khan to introduce 'tourist tax' in London up to 5% of hotel room cost
author: Nicholas Cecil
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) ![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png) Lord Khan said: “I strongly welcome the Government giving London the power to introduce an Overnight Visitor Levy. “This needs to happen sooner rather than later.” ![

Sir Sadiq Khan is expected to decide next year whether to stand for re-election as London Mayor in 2028

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/03/14/01M1KBH1NTHYDTC0Q4A7P15533.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) He added: “London’s visitor economy is a huge success story, supporting jobs, businesses and investment across the capital and the wider country, and I have long argued that London should have the same flexibility as other major global cities to raise and invest funding locally.” However, he risks a row with business chiefs who have called for the new levy to be set at a flat rate of £2 to £3 rather than a percentage of the cost of accommodation, given hotels are far more expensive in London than many other cities. The Standard understands that the tax will be set at no more than 5% of the cost of rooms. Lord Khan added: “A well-designed, modest levy has the potential to provide an important additional source of funding to support growth, strengthen London’s offer to visitors and help us remain globally competitive. “It would allow us to reinvest in the places, infrastructure, culture and experiences that make London one of the world’s greatest cities to visit, while helping manage the pressures that come with welcoming tens of millions of visitors every year.” There are also concerns in the hospitality sector that the funds raised will not be used to increase tourism. But the London Mayor, who was meeting Communities Secretary Angela Rayner with other mayors in No10 North in Manchester on Thursday, insisted: “I will work closely with London’s boroughs, accommodation providers, hospitality and tourism businesses and other partners, before final decisions are taken.” Ministers backed a percentage rather than flat rate charge to protect budget holidays and cheaper hotels. In Scotland, Edinburgh has introduced a tourist tax of 5% of the cost of a room, which will be charged on the first five nights of a visitor's stay. Read More Glasgow is also bringing in a 5% levy, and Aberdeen 7%. But hotel prices are far higher in London than in Scotland, Berlin and many other European cities and a 5% levy would put on average £11.50 a night on the cost of staying in the capital, with the average hotel price being £230, according to industry research, though this varies depending on the time of year. Lisbon has a flat four euros (£3.52) levy, up to a maximum of seven nights, or 28 euros (£24.67) for all types of accommodation. Reacting to Lord Khan’s move, the leader of Westminster City Council voiced concern that London could lose out to other rival capitals. Councillor Paul Swaddle said: “The reality about an overnight visitor levy is that in Europe, VAT is significantly lower and the total tax burden is lower. Our hotels across the West End and elsewhere in Westminster need to be competitive to keep us a global visitor attraction.”
summary: London Mayor Sadiq Khan plans to introduce a tourist tax of up to 5% on hotel room costs following the Government's decision to grant London the power to levy an Overnight Visitor Levy. While ministers back the percentage-based charge to protect cheaper accommodations, business chiefs and hospitality representatives have raised concerns over competitiveness and how the funds will be used. Similar levies have already been adopted in Scottish cities such as Edinburgh, Glasgow, and Aberdeen.
key_points: London Mayor Sadiq Khan is introducing an Overnight Visitor Levy set at no more than 5% of hotel room costs.
Business leaders and the hospitality sector have expressed concern that a percentage-based tax will disproportionately harm London's competitiveness compared to cities with flat-rate fees.
Ministers supported the percentage charge rather than a flat rate to protect budget holidays and cheaper hotels.
A 5% levy in London would add an average of £11.50 per night to a stay, based on an average hotel price of £230.
Similar tourist taxes of 5% to 7% have already been introduced in Scottish cities including Edinburgh, Glasgow, and Aberdeen.

title: Crime concerns outweigh reality, King's College London study finds
author: Amy Clarke
content:
![London Mayor Sadiq Khan, wearing a dark suit and white shirt, gestures while speaking to a uniformed police officer in the street, with several people blurred in the background.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/db29/live/a4b78120-9c7d-11f0-95c6-7592d7636e22.jpg)
Mayor Sir Sadiq Khan said the study was "a sad indictment of the volume of misinformation"
- Published
People are overestimating how much crime takes place in London and how unsafe residents feel, according to research by King's College London., external
Researchers found that respondents thought that 30% of Londoners had personally experienced a crime in the year between October 2024 and September 2025, when the reality was 12.2%, according to ONS figures.
Londoners involved in the survey also overestimated the risk, putting the figure at 25%.
While perceptions did not always match the data, the figures suggest many Londoners continue to have concerns about safety.
The 12.2% figure still means roughly one in eight people had been the victim of a crime, while 37% of residents say they do not feel safe walking alone in their area after dark.
So what does the research tell us about the gap between how safe London actually is and how safe people think it is?
What the figures show
The findings are based on two YouGov surveys of 2,164 and 3,969 adults carried out between 23 and 27 March 2026 as part of the Mistaken Britain research programme.
Researchers compared respondents' perceptions with data from the Crime Survey for England and Wales, Home Office crime figures and official surveys on how safe Londoners feel in their local areas.
Half of respondents thought London had the highest rate of violent crime of any region in the year to September 2025.
In fact, the research found that police-recorded crime data showed London had the lowest rate of violent crime of any region in England and Wales.
Nearly two-thirds of people (62%) believed overall crime in London had increased between 2019 and 2025 when in reality, it had fallen slightly by 1.4%.
Four in 10 thought murders had risen, despite the number falling by around 15% over the same period.
Respondents also overestimated how unsafe Londoners feel.
They believed 60% of residents do not feel safe walking alone in their local area after dark, when in reality, this figure was 37%.
Londoners themselves slightly overestimated the level of concern, with residents estimating that half of Londoners feel unsafe in those circumstances.
'Lies and hatred'
However, the research found people were often right about rises in specific offences.
Most correctly identified increases in shoplifting and theft from the person, both of which more than doubled between 2019 and 2025.
A majority also correctly said they felt sexual offences and violence against the person had increased.
More recent Metropolitan Police figures show sexual offences rose by 4.2% and violence against the person by 7.0% in the year to July 2026.
The Metropolitan Police has recently stepped up efforts to tackle phone theft, saying offences in the West End halved between June 2025 and June 2026 following a crackdown and a doubling of patrols in the area.
The force said its largest-ever operation targeting phone theft resulted in 13,000 fewer mobile phones being stolen across London.
![A close up of a group of people using mobile phones - their hands and the phones are visible.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/df09/live/f702e070-67d2-11f1-9c4b-77e30dd66647.jpg)
A March GLA report warned of "disinformation" about the capital on social media
The mayor of London and the Greater London Authority (GLA) had previously raised concerns about the way the capital is portrayed online.
A GLA report published in March found social media users were being targeted by "disinformation" about the capital.
It said online activity describing London as a dangerous city in decline increased by between 150% and 200% between March 2024 and March 2026, while migration-related narratives referencing London rose by more than 350%.
Sir Sadiq launched a Â£7m campaign in June to showcase London to the world and tackle online disinformation.
Susan Hall, the leader of the City Hall Tories, previously said that the mayor "should spend more time trying to fix things as opposed to saying, 'La la la la la', I'm not listening, everything's fine.'"
Sir Sadiq said the city had been subjected to a "relentless and unprecedented attack of lies and hatred" on social media.
The mayor said of the new study: "This latest research from King's College is a sad indictment of the volume of misinformation and organised disinformation being peddled against our capital.
"For too long we have seen foreign state actors, politicians, bots and others regularly talking down London, taking advantage of the outrage economy which allows people to profit from the poison, algorithms and rage-baiting spread online."
The mayor said investment in the Met and the Violence Reduction Unit had helped drive a 14% fall in neighbourhood crime.
"But I'm clear that one crime is one too many and am determined to build on the progress we have achieved by being tough on crime", adding that this would be backed by "record investment in front-line policing".
UK's 'most polarising city'
The findings come amid a wider debate about how London is portrayed in politics, the media and online.
In an interview with GB News last week, US President Donald Trump claimed London was a "much different place", with "crime that's very high".
He went on to say: "You have areas in Paris and London where the police don't want to even go in them, there's no law and order. They're afraid to go in them.
"Either they're afraid or they just don't, you know, they don't want to lose their life."
London is described by the King's College London report as the UK's most polarising city.
While 42% of respondents view it favourably, 36% view it unfavourably, a much narrower gap than for other major UK cities.
More than half (54%) think London has changed for the worse since 2016, while only 16% think it has changed for the better.
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external
summary: A study by King's College London reveals that people significantly overestimate crime rates and personal safety risks in London compared to official statistics. Researchers found that respondents believed violent crime and overall crime were rising when official data showed decreases, although the public correctly identified increases in specific offenses like shoplifting and theft. Mayor Sadiq Khan attributed the distorted perceptions to a high volume of misinformation and online disinformation targeting the capital.
key_points: Respondents thought 30% of Londoners experienced a crime between October 2024 and September 2025, whereas the actual ONS figure was 12.2%.
Police-recorded crime data showed London had the lowest rate of violent crime of any region in England and Wales, contrary to the belief of half the survey respondents.
Overall crime in London fell slightly by 1.4% between 2019 and 2025, while nearly two-thirds of respondents believed it had increased.
The public correctly identified increases in shoplifting and theft from the person, which both more than doubled between 2019 and 2025.
A Greater London Authority report found that online activity describing London as dangerous increased by 150% to 200% between March 2024 and March 2026.

title: ‘Landmark’ Wimbledon home given to National Trust
author: Pierra Willix
content:
The National Trust has been given 22 Parkside, the influential Wimbledon home designed by Richard Rogers that inspired Paris’s Centre Pompidou and the Lloyd’s of London building.
Described by the heritage trust as a "landmark example of 20th-century design" and "one of the most significant homes in British architectural history", 22 Parkside was created by Rogers alongside his wife Su Rogers, who was also an architect.
Built between 1968 and 1970 for his parents, Nino and Dada Rogers, the house has moved from private ownership to the conservation charity, which stated it will "protect one of the UK’s most important examples of modern architecture for future generations".
The home is widely credited with helping inspire the Centre Pompidou in Paris and shaping the design of London's Lloyd’s building.
![](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/09/12/01M22WV4MNXT6Z18K8CY5NWXYV.jpg)
Ben Rogers, the son of Richard and Su Rogers, said: "22 Parkside is much more than a family home. It is one of the most important buildings my father and mother created – a place where many of the ideas that would go on to influence my father’s work and some of the world’s most celebrated architecture were first tested and explored.
"As a family, we wanted to ensure that this remarkable house would be protected, cared for and shared with future generations, rather than remaining a private asset. The National Trust brings the expertise, public purpose and long-term commitment needed to safeguard its future, while opening up its story to students, researchers and visitors."
![It has been called a ‘landmark example of 20th century design’](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/09/11/09105930-7920f561-bb8d-4999-b19c-5caa72c35bb2.jpg)
Ruthie Rogers, who was married to the architect from 1973 until his death at age 88 in 2021, noted her late husband "regarded public access to culture – whether architecture, art, theatre, music, or design – as one of the great aspirations in life".
She said: "It filled him with such joy that the public would have access to this house that was once private, a house that was a prototype for what he thought houses could be for all."
National Trust director-general Hilary McGrady said: "We are profoundly grateful to the Rogers family for placing this extraordinary house in our care. Their generosity means that 22 Parkside will now become part of our shared inheritance, belonging not to a single family but to the people of England, Wales and Northern Ireland.
"This extraordinary gift will ensure that a building where world-changing ideas were born continues to inspire new generations of thinkers, makers and creators."
![It inspired the Centre Pompidou and Lloyd’s of London](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/09/11/09110025-f1716377-1358-411d-a16e-8235d3deba4d.jpg)
The charity plans to organise guided tours, educational initiatives and interactive digital content at the site, aiming for it to "becomes a creative and educational resource for schools, universities and other heritage organisations around the world".
The property will open to the public this Saturday as part of London’s Open House festival.
Positioned on a narrow, wooded plot adjacent to Wimbledon Common in south-west London, the residence used a pioneering approach to modern construction, flexible living and light-filled interiors.
Constructed as separate single-storey pavilions surrounding a central courtyard, the house and studio provided privacy while maintaining a link to the surrounding garden and using natural light.
![The National Trust has said the home is a place where ‘world-changing ideas were born’](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/09/09/11/09110124-5bb53608-4ee0-4e2f-a558-0f50ddea9350.jpg)
Granted Grade II* listed status in 2013, it is also known as the Rogers House or Wimbledon House.
Rogers was also celebrated for other major architectural projects, including the Channel 4 Building in Westminster, law courts in Strasbourg, Bordeaux and Antwerp, the National Assembly of Wales in Cardiff, Barajas Airport in Madrid and Terminal 5 at Heathrow Airport.
summary: The National Trust has been given 22 Parkside in Wimbledon, a landmark 20th-century home designed by architects Richard and Su Rogers. Built between 1968 and 1970, the property served as a prototype for ideas that later influenced world-famous structures like Paris's Centre Pompidou and London's Lloyd’s building. The conservation charity plans to open the Grade II* listed house to the public and use it as an educational and creative resource.
key_points: The influential Wimbledon home, 22 Parkside, was designed by Richard and Su Rogers and built between 1968 and 1970.
The property inspired architectural concepts used in the Centre Pompidou in Paris and the Lloyd’s of London building.
The Rogers family gifted the house to the National Trust to protect it and share its history with future generations.
The property will open to the public this Saturday as part of London’s Open House festival.

title: Private hospital’s failures ‘contributed to death of Sir Richard Branson’s wife’
author: Sam Hall
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Richard Branson announces death of wife Joan Templeman](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/09/18/09175003-10752618-5b9a-4088-b206-4e367b263533.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![WEST END FINAL](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_we_final_embed_desktop.png)
A private hospital’s failure to provide preventative medication contributed to the death of Sir Richard Branson’s wife, an inquest has concluded.
Read More
Westminster Coroner’s Court heard on Wednesday that she died after suffering a pulmonary embolism, a sudden, dangerous blockage in a lung artery, resulting from deep vein thrombosis.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/09/18/902fdf93e67b73742d78272ebf029b73Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5MDU5MDgz-2.1285088.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
The virtual inquest heard that Lady Joan was admitted to the hospital on November 17 after a fall weeks earlier on Necker Island – a private luxury retreat in the Caribbean’s British Virgin Islands owned by her billionaire husband.
Lady Joan described the fall to her GP as “tripping over some slippers by the bed” and was diagnosed with sustained fractures of the pelvis and fractures of the right hip, the virtual inquest heard.
Haematologist Dr George Adams told the inquest that Lady Joan was “extremely high risk” for blood clots and the “biggest risk factor by far was her immobility and her fracture”.
Glasgow-born Lady Joan did not receive any prophylactic anticoagulation – the preventative use of treatments to stop dangerous blood clots from forming – from her hospital admission to her death.
Dr Adams said he believed this contributed to her death, saying prophylactic anticoagulation “reduces the number of clots and the size of those clots”, adding: “More likely than not, it would have reduced the chances of her having a fatal pulmonary embolism.”
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/09/18/af1c7478bda04c9ceab77f65b86e6962Y29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5MDU5MDgz-2.12077452.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
The Imperial academic, who was not involved in Lady Joan’s care, added that “appropriate anticoagulation” would have “probably prevented her from dying”.
Professor Fiona Wilcox, senior coroner for Inner West London, described Lady Joan as a “wonderful woman” who was “unfailingly kind”.
Giving her conclusion, Professor Wilcox said it was “not a case of neglect” and there “wasn’t an absence of treatment”.
The coroner said Lady Joan did not receive prophylactic anticoagulants at the hospital despite a “very high risk of developing deep vein thrombosis”.
Giving her conclusion, the coroner said: “I do find her death would have likely been prevented and the lack of anticoagulation did cause or contribute to her death probably.”
Lady Joan also did not receive an immediate Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) assessment to check her risk of developing harmful blood clots, the inquest heard.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/09/18/25ad126063ccd76aa22a2d303df3c02cY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5MDU5MDgz-2.1075041.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Dr Adams said “any patient who comes into hospital should have an immediate VTE assessment to determine their risk of bleeding”.
Lady Joan’s daughter, Dr Holly Branson, told the inquest that her mother also did not have Thrombo-Embolus Deterrent stockings – which are designed to prevent deep vein thrombosis by promoting blood flow in the lower legs – for the first 48 hours after being admitted.
The hospital’s admitting doctor, Dr Basir Kunduzi, did not complete a bleeding risk assessment on the day of her admission, the inquest heard.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/09/18/5634afb0325163d74db9168c1e488e2eY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5MDU5MDgz-2.5050574.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
Dr Kunduzi said Lady Joan “should have been on anti-coagulants” and her death led him to “reflect on my role as a doctor” and the importance of “good communication between team members”.
Resident medical officer Dr Nevil Pavithran, who was also involved in Lady Joan’s care, told the inquest that she “should have received her first dose of anticoagulation prophylaxis within 12 hours of admission”, adding this not occurring caused a “significant risk”.
The doctor said he had “spent quite a lot of time going over the incidents” and said he felt he “should have been more forceful”.
Lady Joan’s consultant, Dr Inaki Bovil, said there had been a “lot of work at the Lister to make it more robust around VTE and risk prevention” and to “prevent this from happening again”.
![](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/09/09/18/7015f585294c626d76f4f3fa43c7baabY29udGVudHNlYXJjaGFwaSwxNzg5MDQ2OTQx-2.12077477.jpg?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
After her death, Sir Richard described his wife as the “shining star around which our family’s universe has always orbited”.
Paying tribute to Lady Joan, Sir Richard wrote: “Life will never be the same without her. But we have 50 incredible years of memories – years filled with tears and laughter, kindness and a love that shaped our family more than words could ever capture.
“It was a relationship that worked. We just had lots of laughs. We were very lucky.”
summary: An inquest concluded that a private hospital's failure to provide preventative medication contributed to the death of Sir Richard Branson's wife, Lady Joan. Lady Joan died from a pulmonary embolism resulting from deep vein thrombosis after being admitted with pelvic and hip fractures. The coroner and medical experts stated that appropriate anticoagulation and an immediate risk assessment would have likely prevented her death.
key_points: Lady Joan died from a pulmonary embolism resulting from deep vein thrombosis following hospital admission for pelvic and hip fractures.
An inquest heard that she did not receive prophylactic anticoagulation treatments or an immediate VTE assessment upon admission.
Medical experts testified that appropriate preventative medication would have likely prevented her death.
The coroner concluded it was not a case of neglect, but that the lack of anticoagulation contributed to her death.

title: One of London’s most beloved off-West End theatres has closed for good
author: Andrzej Lukowski
content:
[title]
Sad news today as the Gate Theatre announces that it is closing all operations, the end to an almost 50-year-history.
Founded in 1979 above the Prince Albert Pub in Notting Hill, the Gate was a dynamic, international work-focussed theatre that served as a peer of other major off-West End venues like the Bush and Hampstead theatres. Some heavyweight British stage directors have run it on their way to the top, notably Stephen Daldry, Thea Sharrock, Carrie Cracknell and Ellen McDougall.
Unfortunately it’s now over. It’s sad but not a surprise. Unlike the Bush and Hampstead, the Gate never made it to a more modern new venue: it hung on it at Prince Albert for over 40 years, but closed during the pandemic. In 2023, citing the poor accessibility of its original venue, it took up residence in the larger Theatro Technis venue in Camden, but this was a complicated building share arrangement that greatly reduced the amount of shows it could stage. It also lost its Arts Council funding in 2022, and McDougall – its final permanent artistic director – departed in 2021.
It did produce a series of acclaimed shows in the post-Notting Hill era, including 2024’s Wish You Were Here, staged at Theatro Technis, and last year’s Scenes from the Climate Era, staged at the Playground Theatre.
The official press release announcing its closure states that ‘after several years of short-term success it has become apparent that this is not sustainable in the long-term’. That’s a bit vague but it’s fairly apparent that despite the team’s heroic efforts, the Gate no longer has the means to stage the sort of year-round programme it once did and that successful individual shows weren’t enough to keep the organisation afloat.
Speaking personally as Time Out’s theatre editor, I’ll really miss the weird and provocative work the Gate used to stage, and I’ll miss its eccentric, cramped old venue, which accounted for about 90 percent of the times I have ever been to Notting Hill. But it’s obvious why an attempt was made to move somewhere bigger and move accessible and it is, unfortunately, rotten luck that it was looking to move house in the aftermath of a pandemic and a round of Arts Council funding that was famously harsh on London companies. That the Gate continued to stage good work against the odds afterwards is really impressive, but you can of course see why its creative and management team called it quits – but they didn’t go down quietly.
